title: Port: ruby and tawny
subtitle: Two ways of ageing
objectives: Explain the Douro's role in Port

steps.title: Douro and Gaia
steps.body: Port grapes grow in the Douro's three sub-regions: the Baixo Corgo, coolest and wettest; the Cima Corgo, heart of quality; and the Douro Superior, hottest and driest. Vineyards are classified A to F. The wine traditionally travelled down to the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, across from Porto, for cool, humid ageing.
steps.highlight: Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo, Douro Superior

steps.title: Ruby and tawny
steps.body: Ruby Ports age in large vats, with little oxygen, keeping colour and fruit. Reserve Ruby is a better selection. Tawny Ports age in small 550-litre casks, called pipes, where oxygen turns them brown and nutty. Aged tawny with an indication of age, 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 years, is a blend tasted to match that style. Colheita is a single-vintage tawny.
steps.highlight: Vats for ruby; pipes for tawny

options: A tawny from a single vintage
steps.explanation: Colheita is a single-vintage tawny aged at least 7 years in cask.

steps.title: White and rosé
steps.body: White Port, from white grapes like Malvasia Fina and Gouveio, ranges from dry to sweet; mixed with tonic, it's a classic aperitif in Porto. Rosé Port, approved in 2008, is made with short skin contact and drunk young and chilled. Aged white Ports, with age indications, also exist.

steps.prompt: Match each Port to its ageing.
steps.explanation: Ageing in vat or cask defines the family.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Port grapes grow in the Douro's three sub-regions
Ruby ages in large vats; tawny in small casks
Colheita is a single-vintage tawny; white and rosé Ports exist
